source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 27 2026, ANSWERS.md, Garden): Sun Life uXperience Design Jam, November 2, 2024 (University of Waterloo Stratford School news article; PDF schedule: one day, 6.5 hours working time, 3-minute presentations). Team of six (slide 558:7010): Gaurav Shah, Emily Chan, Charlene Lee, Winston Zhao, Darren Millar and Andrew Ellyatt. No award, so no Result row and no placing. Winston designed the app screens and the basic design system (not the tree and flower art, the slides, the Bento or the banner). The HMW is Sun Life’s prompt, word for word. Deliverables: clickable prototype and live pitch. The three rougher home screens are his earlier versions. Garden is its own app that links people to Sun Life products and advisors. Lessons he chose: pitch it as a story; make progress visible. Everything else is read from the PDF (brief, workshops, Sarah’s story, the four-part concept, the whiteboard) and the screens (text quoted as it appears). Story pass (Nov 27 2026, ANSWERS.md): why a chat (less intimidating, beginner friendly, personal); why a garden (progress you can see, grows with you, brand and mascot, real-world impact); Home changes (bars felt like numbers; rewards up front); team split like the PDF roles, Winston the UI designer who set up the design system and designed the screens (the other UI designer: illustrations, per the PDF roles); look (green for growth, sunflower yellow for Sun Life’s slogan, serif headings and soft colours so it feels friendly and calm, not like a bank). The quick first steps and behavioural economics come from the PDF script; “make it less human” is written next to “afraid to reach out” on the whiteboard. No judge feedback.

fields.description: Savings plans that bloom as you reach each goal.
fields.intro: Garden is a money app for young Canadians: tell it what you’re saving for, and it builds a plan of small steps and grows flowers and trees as you go. In a team of six at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam 2024, I designed the app screens and a basic design system.
fields.summary: Designing a savings app that breaks big money goals into small steps and grows a garden as you reach them.
fields.overview: Garden is for young Canadians like Sarah, a busy student saving for her first car. Our team of six designed it in one day at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam, and we presented it as Sarah’s story in a three-minute live pitch.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we help young Canadians find, and use the financial tools & education available to them?
content: This was Sun Life’s prompt at the uXperience Design Jam, held at the University of Waterloo’s Stratford School on November 2, 2024. Six of us had about six and a half hours to answer it, with a three-minute pitch at the end.

Sun Life’s brief was simple: there are financial tools and education to help young people make money decisions and plan for their goals, but they’re under-used. They asked for something easy and inclusive that helps young Canadians open up about money and feel confident about their financial future.
There were also two workshops that morning: one on financial fluency and one on breaking down barriers with behavioural economics.

We split the work like a small product team: one of us on product, one writing the script, one making the slides and two on UI. I set up the design system and designed the app screens, and the other UI designer made the illustrations.

sections.title: Persona
sections.heading: Meet Sarah
content: We told the whole pitch through one person. Sarah is a second-year GBDA student at Waterloo with a long commute to Stratford, so she wants a car, but the $2,000 down payment feels like a mountain.

content.caption: Everything competing for Sarah’s time, from our pitch.

content: Between five courses, a part-time job and her friends, money planning keeps getting pushed back. She has never saved this much before and doesn’t know where to start. A chequing account? A high-interest savings account?
Sarah isn’t alone. On our whiteboard, we listed what gets in the way for young people like her, and most of what follows comes back to this list.

content.caption: The problems we listed, from the whiteboard.

sections.title: Idea
sections.heading: Big goals, small steps
content: Before any screens, there was a whiteboard. Around Sun Life’s question, we listed why young people don’t use financial tools: the time it takes, fear, procrastination and relying on parents. Then came the functions we wanted, visual ideas and the problems above.

content.alt: A whiteboard covered in red marker: Sun Life’s How might we question at the top, then Why not?, Functions, Visual components, a script outline for Sarah, a Growth column (start with a sapling, plant a tree, grow your own forest), Problems, Gamification and Constraints with AI generated advice
content.caption: Our whiteboard from the day.

content: The idea we landed on was Garden. It takes one big goal and breaks it into small steps you can act on:

bullets: **Make a plan** from a goal, in your own words.
**Keep track** of your progress as you save.
**Find resources** for each step: answers in the app, outside resources and a financial advisor.
**Act on the plan** in the app, like saving into a new account.

content: Progress shows up as a garden: smaller goals grow flowers, and saving and learning grow trees. We built the whole app around it for four reasons:

bullets: **Progress you can see.** Plants growing feel like progress in a way charts and numbers don’t, and numbers were on our list of problems.
**It grows with you.** Saving is slow, like a garden. As Sarah grows, Garden grows with her.
**A brand to remember.** The pitch tips we worked from asked for a fun brand with custom illustrations, and a garden gave us one.
**Real-world impact.** When your virtual tree is fully grown, a real one gets planted, so the progress means something outside the app.

content: Garden is its own app, and it points people to Sun Life’s products and advisors along the way.

content.alt: An iPhone showing Garden’s first home screen: Hello, Sarah; Welcome to your Garden with Create a plan, Find resources and Earn badges; and About your Garden, explaining Trees (a real tree is planted after your virtual tree is grown) and Flowers for smaller goals
content.caption: Before the first plan, Home explains how the garden works.

sections.title: Plan
sections.heading: Planning by chat
content: Anxiety with starting was on our list, and it’s Sarah’s problem too: she doesn’t know which account she needs, let alone how to plan for a car. So planning in Garden starts as a chat. We chose a chat for three reasons:

bullets: **It’s less intimidating.** Typing a goal in your own words is easier than a form full of money fields.
**It’s beginner friendly.** You don’t need to know which account or product you need to start.
**It’s personal.** Garden asks follow-up questions to fit the plan to you.

content: Sarah types “I need to save $2000 for a car”. Garden asks about her timeline, her income and her saving style, then lays out a Car Savings Plan: $500 every three months, $2,000 over 12 months.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: Create a plan with example goals; Sarah’s message “I need to save $2000 for a car” and Garden asking about Timeline, Your income and Saving style; then the Car Savings Plan with four $500 steps from November 2024 to November 2025, March open with its explanation, and Save and activate plan
content.caption: From a goal to a plan in two messages.

content: Each step opens to explain itself, like why it’s $500 every three months, and the Save and activate plan button turns it on.

The first steps are quick on purpose. Drawing on behavioural economics, the plan puts easy steps first to build momentum: in our pitch, Sarah opens a high-interest savings account, links it to Garden and sets up automatic transfers in a few minutes.

sections.title: Garden
sections.heading: Watch it grow
content: Here is where “overwhelmed with numbers” gets its answer. Every plan lives in the Plans tab. Big plans get cards with their total, the next goal and a plant that grows with them. Smaller ones, like a MacBook Pro or a Mexico trip, sit in a list, each with a flower at its own stage.
A toggle at the top switches Plans to Garden, where everything you’ve grown is planted together. Sarah’s garden starts with two flowers and fills in as she finishes goals.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: the Plans tab with cards for Buy Car, Buy House, Retirement Plan and Student Loans, a list of smaller plans (MacBook Pro, Mexico Trip, New Tattoo), each with a flower at its stage, and a New button; the Garden view with two yellow flowers; and the Garden view with a big green tree, a yellow tulip, a sunflower and sprouts
content.caption: Plans, then the garden as it grows.

sections.title: Home
sections.heading: Hello, Sarah
content: Each time Sarah opens Garden, she lands on Home. It leads with a pinned goal, then recent plans with their progress and the badges she has earned, like 500 Saver and 1k Saver.

Home went through three rougher versions before the final one, and two of them are shown here. Plain progress bars read like the numbers we were trying to get away from, so plans moved to dotted timelines that end in a plant icon showing each plan’s stage. The final home also put the rewards up front, with a flower on the goal card and badges below the plans, and Search got its own tab.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: an early home with a New MacBook Pro card and plain progress bars for Retirement and Student Loan; another early version with Plans as dotted timelines ending in plant icons and an Ask button; and the final home with a sunflower on the goal card, Recent Plans, earned badges and a Search tab
content.caption: Two earlier versions of Home, then the final one.

sections.title: Support
sections.heading: Help along the way
content: Two more problems on our list were being afraid to reach out and finance feeling intimidating to younger users. Next to the first, our whiteboard says “make it less human”. Garden’s answer is to teach as well as track.
Resources holds knowledge cards on topics like OSAP loans, GICs, savings and buying a car, each with its own minigames. A list below covers leasing a house, mutual funds and retirement.

Search takes questions in plain words, like “How do I open a savings account?” Its answers come from Garden’s resource bank, and a note under the questions says Search doesn’t generate new data or store yours.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Resources with Search Knowledge Cards, cards for OSAP Loans, What is a GIC?, Savings and Buying a Car with their minigame counts, and a list of Leasing a house, Mutual Funds and Retirement; and Search with How can we help?, three suggested questions and a note that Garden Search answers from a resource bank

content: Garden also reaches Sarah outside the app. In our pitch, two years after her car, a widget on her home screen asks if she’s considered an emergency fund.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: a phone home screen with a Garden widget asking “Have you considered an emergency fund?”, then Garden’s home with the same suggestion in a green card at the top
content.caption: The widget, then the same nudge on Home.

content: On Home, the same suggestion sits at the top, based on her journey so far. A lock-screen notification can do the same: “Pssst... have you considered an emergency fund?”

sections.title: Design system
sections.heading: A friendly money app
content: As one of the two UI designers, I set up Garden’s design system and designed every screen with it. I wanted Garden to feel friendly and calm, not like a bank:

bullets: **Green for growth.** Garden green ties the app to plants, growth and money.
**Sunflower yellow for Sun Life.** It nods to Sun Life’s slogan, “Life’s brighter under the sun”.
**Warm type.** Hedvig Letters Serif for headings, with Inter for everything else and soft colours around them.
**Progress that shows its stage.** Each plan’s dotted timeline ends in a plant icon that shows how far along it is.

content.alt: Garden’s design system on one panel: colour swatches for Garden green #399C74, Mint #C2E0D4, Sunflower #EDBC33, Forest #184231 and Warm grey #64615B; type samples, “Hello, Sarah” in Hedvig Letters Serif and “New MacBook Pro” in Inter; and three components from the app: the New MacBook Pro goal card, the plan list with dotted timelines and plant icons, and the Home, Plans, Resources and Search tab bar
content.caption: Colours, type and components from the final screens.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: Results and lessons
content: We presented Garden in a three-minute live pitch, told as Sarah’s story. It followed her from a $2,000 down payment that felt like a mountain to reaching her goal six months later, then two years on to an emergency fund. Alongside the pitch, we made a clickable prototype of the app.

bullets: **Pitch it as a story.** Following Sarah made the features make sense in three minutes.
**Make progress visible.** Flowers and trees make saving feel like progress, not just numbers.

content: Garden started with Sun Life’s question and one overwhelmed student. For the anxiety of starting, it plans by chat and puts quick steps first. For the numbers, it grows a garden. In one day, our team of six turned that into a clickable prototype and a three-minute story.
